title: How to Stop China from Freeriding on American AI
gist: Fedasiuk argues Washington should sanction Chinese labs for industrial-scale distillation attacks — fraud under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, not the legitimate technique of distillation — citing Anthropic tracing over 3.4 million exchanges to Moonshot AI via hundreds of fake accounts, and pairs enforcement with an FTC 'nutrition label' for model provenance and federal advance purchase commitments to build American open-weight competitors.

themes.theme: Chinese Open Weights Now Dominate Global Workloads

insights.claim: Chinese open-source AI models now account for the majority of global AI workloads, marching steadily into global markets.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Majority global workload share means Chinese open models are already the default inference substrate — a direct revenue headwind for U.S. frontier labs in price-sensitive markets.
insights.quote: China’s open-source AI models are marching steadily into global markets, and now account for the majority of global AI workloads.
insights.locator: China’s open-source AI models are marching

insights.claim: Developers choose Qwen and Kimi for hard economic reasons — the models are free, permissively licensed, easy to fine-tune, and cheap to serve — not out of ignorance or ideology.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Any American open-weight competitor must match free, permissive, fine-tunable, and cheap-to-serve on all four axes or it will not displace Chinese models.
insights.quote: They are choosing them because the models are free, permissively licensed, easy to fine-tune, and cheap to serve.
insights.locator: Finally, both the U.S. government and U.S. frontier labs

insights.claim: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has declared American companies should 'absolutely' use Chinese models that beat American counterparts on price, putting a major U.S. hardware vendor on the pro-diffusion side of the debate.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Nvidia's incentive is inference volume regardless of model origin — expect it to lobby against restrictions that U.S. model labs favor.
insights.quote: Industry has been vocal about its own views, with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang declaring that American companies should “absolutely” use Chinese models that outcompete American counterparts on price.
insights.locator: Industry has been vocal about its own views

insights.claim: Foundational software today is being written by San Francisco engineers using Chinese models answerable to state security services, and elite American startups are routing proprietary code through Chinese models without their customers' knowledge.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Undisclosed Chinese model dependency is a latent liability for enterprise customers and insurers — provenance disclosure would reprice vendor risk overnight.
insights.quote: Foundational software today is being written by software engineers in San Francisco using Chinese models answerable to state security services.
insights.locator: The economic displacement of American AI compounds

themes.theme: Distillation as Technique vs. Extraction as Fraud

insights.claim: Distillation — training a smaller student model on a stronger teacher's outputs — is an industry-standard method used by every AI lab including American frontier labs, so banning it is not technically enforceable because anyone with output access can rearrange outputs into training data.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Policy proposals to ban distillation outright are unenforceable and should be discounted; only fraud-based enforcement is actionable.
insights.quote: Banning distillation is not technically enforceable, as anyone with access to a model’s output, including legitimate customers, can rearrange those outputs back into training data.
insights.locator: Distillation as Technique, Extraction as Fraud

insights.claim: An American AI ecosystem confined to producing un-distillable models would artificially protect only two or three frontier labs at the expense of every other AI developer.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Anti-distillation rules would function as regulatory capture favoring incumbents — a real risk factor for the mid-tier American model and application layer.
insights.quote: an American AI ecosystem confined to producing un-distillable models would artificially protect two or three frontier labs at the expense of every other AI developer seeking to adapt scientific innovation
insights.locator: Even if it were possible to stop distillation outright

insights.claim: Distillation explains less of Chinese model performance than Washington believes: DeepSeek R1's January 2025 efficiency breakthrough came primarily from a reinforcement learning change, and Moonshot's agent swarming in 2026 was a homegrown capability.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Stopping distillation attacks will slow but not stop Chinese progress — do not underwrite a thesis that enforcement restores a U.S. capability lead.
insights.quote: DeepSeek R1’s efficiency breakthrough in January 2025 came primarily from a change in reinforcement learning rather than from copying American competitors.
insights.locator: Second, distillation does not explain as much

insights.claim: The legally actionable line is a 'distillation attack' — obtaining competitor access through deception with fabricated identities, purpose-built evasion infrastructure, and systematic circumvention of security controls — which falls under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and wire fraud statutes rather than civil contract law.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Criminal fraud statutes, not IP law, are the enforcement vector to watch — that determines which Chinese labs face real sanctions exposure.
insights.quote: a fraudulent scheme to gain and sustain unauthorized access —including the use of fabricated identities, purpose-built evasion infrastructure, and systematic circumvention of security controls — is the domain of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and wire fraud statutes
insights.locator: Third, the objectionable conduct of Chinese AI labs

insights.claim: By February 2026, Anthropic traced more than 3.4 million exchanges with its models to Moonshot, routed through hundreds of fake accounts using an internal platform purpose-built to evade detection.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: This is the concrete forensic record that any sanctions action would rest on — the 3.4 million figure is the benchmark for what 'industrial scale' extraction means.
insights.quote: By February 2026, Anthropic traced more than 3.4 million exchanges with its models to Moonshot.
insights.locator: By February 2026, Anthropic traced

insights.claim: In June, Anthropic told the Senate Banking Committee that Alibaba's Qwen lab had conducted the largest known distillation attack against it to date, putting a second major Chinese lab in the enforcement crosshairs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Alibaba's exposure to U.S. sanctions action is now on the congressional record — a specific, checkable risk for Alibaba's AI business and ADR holders.
insights.quote: Later in June, Anthropic told the Senate Banking Committee that Alibaba’s Qwen lab had conducted the “largest known distillation attack” against it to date.
insights.locator: By February 2026, Anthropic traced

insights.claim: White House science advisor Michael Kratsios stated that Moonshot AI built a sophisticated platform to copy Anthropic's Fable model while evading detection, a day after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the government is finding watermarks of U.S. large language models on many Chinese models.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Both Treasury and the White House science office have publicly committed to the theft narrative — sanctions are a policy question of timing, not of willingness.
insights.quote: The following day, White House science advisor Michael Kratsios clarified that the Chinese AI lab behind K3, Moonshot AI, had built a sophisticated platform to copy Anthropic’s Fable model while evading detection.
insights.locator: The release of the Chinese open-weight AI model Kimi K3

insights.claim: Model outputs are not copyrightable under U.S. law because they lack human authorship, making 'intellectual property theft' a legally dubious description — trade secret law is the better fit.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Legal strategy against Chinese labs will run through trade secret and fraud statutes; copyright-based claims are dead ends and shouldn't drive expectations.
insights.quote: Under U.S. law, model outputs alone are not copyrightable as they require human authorship, which makes “intellectual property theft” a legally dubious description.
insights.locator: Intellectual Property is Only Part of the Story

insights.claim: The protectable trade secret is not any single model response but the underlying model behavior collectively encoded across millions of conversations, which can only be extracted systematically at scale.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: This framing makes query volume the legal trigger — high-volume API scraping becomes the defining evidentiary threshold for enforcement.
insights.quote: the trade secret at issue is not Claude or ChatGPT’s response to a single query, but the underlying model behavior collectively encoded across millions of conversations — which can only be extracted systematically at scale
insights.locator: Skeptics will object that model outputs

insights.claim: The core asymmetry is enforcement jurisdiction: Anthropic was sued in an American court and paid a $1.5 billion copyright settlement for training on pirated books, while there is no forum in which Moonshot will pay anything for extracting Anthropic's trade secrets.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: American labs bear litigation costs their Chinese competitors structurally cannot — a permanent cost asymmetry unless sanctions substitute for courts.
insights.quote: There is no forum in which Moonshot will pay anything for its successful extraction and replication of Anthropic’s trade secrets.
insights.locator: Critics of American frontier labs have already noted

insights.claim: The stronger case against Chinese labs is national security economics, not IP: by converting billions in American compute and reasoning research spend into free releases, Chinese labs undercut American firms in price-sensitive markets worldwide.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: The competitive damage runs through pricing, not capability — U.S. lab revenue in emerging markets is the line item at risk.
insights.quote: By converting billions in American research and development expenditure on compute and machine reasoning research and then releasing the results for free, Chinese labs are undercutting American firms in price-sensitive markets worldwide.
insights.locator: Setting aside the fraud itself

insights.claim: Fedasiuk frames Chinese AI diffusion as free-riding backed by industrial policy — the same playbook China deployed in steel, solar, and shipbuilding, which the United States did not accept in those sectors.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: The steel/solar analogy is the tell for where policy is heading: expect tariff-and-sanction style responses to AI, not free-market forbearance.
insights.quote: It is free-riding backed by industrial policy, the same playbook China has deployed in countless other industries. The United States did not accept this arrangement in steel, solar, or shipbuilding, and should not for AI.
insights.locator: Whether open competition in the AI market is desirable

insights.claim: Beyond price competition, Chinese open models carry three specific national security risks: supply chains vulnerable to poisoned weights that security audits cannot reliably surface, intelligence collection via user traffic routed to servers subject to China's National Intelligence Law, and capability uplift for malicious actors.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Poisoned weights being audit-resistant is the key technical claim — it means no amount of enterprise diligence fully mitigates the risk, favoring provenance restrictions.
insights.quote: supply chains vulnerable to poisoned weights that cannot be reliably surfaced in security audits, intelligence collection through user traffic routed to servers subject to China’s National Intelligence Law, and capability uplift for malicious actors
insights.locator: The economic displacement of American AI compounds

insights.claim: Fedasiuk wants an independent body such as the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation to verify distillation attacks, because attribution evidence has so far come only from victim labs' own forensics — sanctioning a foreign firm on an accuser's internal analysis raises due-process problems.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
entities: Center for AI Standards and Innovation
insights.so_what: Without an independent verifier, sanctions risk being ad-hoc and legally contestable — the creation of that body is the gating step for durable enforcement.
insights.quote: Sanctioning a foreign firm on the strength of an accuser’s internal analysis raises adjudication and due-process questions, and risks ad-hoc statist intervention in the AI market.
insights.locator: Creating a Level Playing Field

insights.claim: Available sanctions instruments include Commerce Entity List designations, IEEPA sanctions, and restrictions on deployment via U.S. cloud infrastructure — which could sever Chinese labs from U.S. cloud, American capital, and critically the Western enterprise customers they are most actively courting.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Cutting off Western enterprise customers is the binding constraint on Chinese lab monetization — that is the sanction that would actually move the commercial needle.
insights.quote: U.S. government action could sever Chinese labs’ access to U.S. cloud infrastructure, American capital, and critically, Western enterprise customers, whom Chinese open-weight labs are most actively courting.
insights.locator: Second, the administration should sanction the labs

insights.claim: The sanctions trigger should be theft of American trade secrets, not technical achievement: labs that train on the open internet or distill from deliberately open models should be treated as fair competition.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: This is a narrow, conduct-based test — it would spare most Chinese open-weight labs, so blanket-ban expectations are likely overpriced.
insights.quote: In any case, the trigger should be based firmly on an entity’s theft of American trade secrets, not technical achievement.
insights.locator: Second, the administration should sanction the labs

insights.claim: Sanctions will not stop determined labs from laundering extraction through API aggregators or labeling firms in third countries — just as export controls have not stopped Chinese compute purchases routed through Southeast Asian shell companies — but they raise cost and lower scale.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Expect a transshipment-intermediary designation regime for AI mirroring the chip one; the middlemen become the enforcement surface.
insights.quote: The Commerce Department could adapt its existing practice of designating transshipment intermediaries on the Entity List to distillation middlemen, forcing offenders to use slower, costlier, smaller-scale channels.
insights.locator: To be sure, adopting a punitive posture

insights.claim: Fedasiuk proposes the FTC require AI services operating in the United States to disclose base model provenance and where user data is processed — a 'nutrition label' for the AI supply chain, previewed by Bessent.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Mandatory model-provenance disclosure would force AI vendors to reveal Chinese dependencies — a near-term compliance catalyst for the application layer.
insights.quote: the Federal Trade Commission should require AI services operating in the United States to disclose the provenance of their base models and where user data is processed — a “nutrition label” for the AI supply chain
insights.locator: Third, to address the legitimate national security risks

insights.claim: Provenance labeling is foundational to enforcing acquisition rules that bar federal agencies and defense contractors from using services built on Chinese models, linking disclosure directly to procurement exclusion.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Disclosure is the precondition for procurement bans — AI vendors selling to government should be assumed to face a Chinese-model exclusion requirement.
insights.quote: Moreover, labeling the use of Chinese models is foundational to enforcing acquisition rules that bar agencies and defense contractors from using services built on top of them.
insights.locator: Third, to address the legitimate national security risks

insights.claim: Bessent named Meta, Nvidia, and Reflection AI in July as the American open-model efforts worth government support.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: These three are the named candidates for federal open-weight support — a specific, checkable watchlist for policy-driven upside.
insights.quote: In off-the-cuff comments in July, Bessent named Meta, Nvidia, and Reflection AI as American open-model efforts worth supporting.
insights.locator: In off-the-cuff comments in July

insights.claim: Congress could pass the long-pending CREATE AI Act, which cleared the House Science Committee unanimously in June, and stand up a dedicated open-weights track within the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource with compute allocations conditioned on permissive licensing.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Unanimous committee passage makes CREATE AI a live legislative catalyst — watch for floor action as a signal of federal compute subsidy flow.
insights.quote: Congress could pass the long-pending CREATE AI Act, which cleared the House Science Committee unanimously in June.
insights.locator: The government has instruments available to support them

insights.claim: Fedasiuk proposes the Pentagon's Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office make an advance commitment to purchase inference and support services for American open-weight models, explicitly modeled on Defense Department purchasing agreements that built the early semiconductor industry by guaranteeing a market for the first expensive chips.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
entities: Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office
insights.so_what: A DoD advance market commitment for open-weight inference would be a direct revenue guarantee — the single most bankable policy proposal here for open-model builders.
insights.quote: Just as Defense Department purchasing agreements built the early semiconductor industry by guaranteeing a market for the first expensive chips, an advance commitment from the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office to purchase inference and support services for American open-weight models would de-risk the private capital those efforts require.
insights.locator: The Pentagon could likewise adapt a tool

insights.claim: The National AI Research Resource Task Force estimated full implementation at $2.6 billion over six years before adding any open-weights track, setting a floor on the fiscal cost of the proposed strategy.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: $2.6 billion over six years is small relative to private AI capex — the constraint on this policy is political will, not money.
insights.quote: The National AI Research Resource Task Force estimated the cost of its full implementation at $2.6 billion over six years, before adding an open-weights track.
insights.locator: None of this comes cheap

insights.claim: The National Science Foundation could extend programs like Pathways to Enable Open-Source Ecosystems to fund a permissively licensed commons of training data and evaluation harnesses — the input most open labs lack by default.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Public training-data commons would lower the entry cost for American open-weight competitors — a structural change to the model supply curve.
insights.quote: And the National Science Foundation, extending existing programs like Pathways to Enable Open-Source Ecosystems, could fund what many open labs lack by default — a permissively licensed commons of training data and related evaluation harnesses.
insights.locator: The Pentagon could likewise adapt a tool

insights.claim: Fedasiuk draws a hard line that protecting Anthropic and OpenAI from theft is a U.S. national security interest but protecting them from competition is not.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: The policy consensus forming is anti-fraud, not pro-incumbent — theses assuming regulatory moats for U.S. frontier labs are on shaky ground.
insights.quote: While protecting Anthropic and OpenAI from theft is a U.S. national security interest, protecting them from competition is not.
insights.locator: While protecting Anthropic and OpenAI from theft

insights.claim: China's extraction campaigns succeeded partly because model APIs remain embarrassingly porous — Anthropic's most restricted model was accessed by Discord hobbyists before its public release, during which hundreds of fake accounts ran millions of queries.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Model access controls are the cheapest fix and are currently failing; expect customer verification and behavioral detection to become a competitive and compliance requirement.
insights.quote: Anthropic’s most restricted model was accessed by Discord hobbyists before its public release, during which time hundreds of fake accounts managed to run millions of queries.
insights.locator: What Frontier Labs Are Responsible For

insights.claim: A company that wants the government to treat its outputs as strategic assets should be expected to secure them like strategic assets — sanctions are a backstop for fraud, not the first line of defense.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Government support for frontier labs will likely come with security obligations attached — a compliance cost to model in, not a free subsidy.
insights.quote: Sanctions are a backstop for fraud, not the first line of defense against it.
insights.locator: What Frontier Labs Are Responsible For

insights.claim: Fedasiuk warns frontier labs against stretching 'distillation attack' into a verbal cudgel against the open AI ecosystem in general, flagging the term's likely rhetorical abuse.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Expect definitional fights over 'distillation attack' to become the front line of AI policy lobbying — the definition determines who gets sanctioned.
insights.quote: The labs should also resist the temptation to stretch the concept of a “distillation attack” into a verbal cudgel against the open AI ecosystem in general.
insights.locator: What Frontier Labs Are Responsible For

insights.claim: The United States will not litigate China out of copying its AI systems; the only decidable question is whether American firms keep funding a frontier that Chinese firms harvest through fraud.
insights.speaker: Ryan Fedasiuk
insights.so_what: Frames the investment question bluntly: without rule enforcement, U.S. frontier R&D spend is a public good subsidizing Chinese competitors.
insights.quote: As with every other technology before, the United States is not going to litigate China out of copying its AI systems.
insights.locator: As with every other technology before
